narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In the 17th century, the polska evolved from courtly set dances into a high-speed partner rotation where couples complete one full turn for every single measure of music.
This is Polska. 17th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (lRl1T7CAD0E)
Title card: Polska · Sweden · 17th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The polska is often traced to the influence of the Polish court in the early 17th century.
Some theories suggest it evolved from earlier Nordic songs or set dances that transitioned into couple-based forms.
on_screen: Map: Sweden · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The polska is a social dance performed in community settings, with specific regional traditions still practiced in parts of Norway and Sweden.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: BEAUTY OF SLAVIC CULTURE (https://archive.org/details/youtube-yMc5b-V7mRI)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is a partner form involving walking promenades and clockwise couple turns.
In many variants, couples rotate once per measure.
Techniques vary by region, including the 'bakmes' (counter-clockwise turn) and the 'pols' turn.
Watch for Pols turn, Bakmes.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (lRl1T7CAD0E)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Couples moving counter-clockwise around the periphery of the room.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is played on standard fiddles or the Hardanger fiddle (hardingfele).
Tunes are typically in triple time, often structured in two eight-bar phrases that are repeated.
Listen for the fiddle, Hardanger fiddle.
The pulse is 3/4.
Triple-meter fiddle music characterized by regional rhythmic nuances, such as long-short beat patterns or smooth, even pulses.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Verified recording — MISSING
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Asymmetrical beats in some variants; others use even sixteenth or eighth notes.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Variants include the Norwegian 'pols' and 'springar', the Swedish 'slängpolska' and 'bondepolska', and various regional styles in Dalarna, Småland, and Jämtland.
The polska is considered a precursor or relative to the hambo and is linked to the polonaise and minuet.
